In this work, we extend these capabilities to demonstrate a practical radiation imaging device in the form of a Compton camera consisting of a SPAD camera and one compact, monolithic scintillator. Our Compton camera prototype successfully reconstructs a gamma-ray source over multiple locations that span a 4$π$ steradian field of view. Our approach is able to resolve two simultaneous events in one monolithic scintillator and enables Compton camera devices with compact, monolithic scintillator volumes for enhanced portability.

title: Decoding Transformer Dynamics via Koopman Subspaces
text: We apply Koopman operator theory and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to characterise how large language models (LLMs) process different input topics. Treating the layer-to-layer evolution of hidden states as a dynamical system, we fit a linear Koopman operator and take the subspace spanned by its dominant modes as a per-topic spectral fingerprint. Four findings emerge. First, the depth map is near-linear: a single linear operator predicts each next-layer state to within approx. 18% relative error (interior variance explained approx. 0.99). Second, over the 57 MMLU subjects the fingerprint is topic-discriminative, matching the MMLU taxonomy at 0.72 nearest-neighbour purity and each subject's semantic neighbourhood at 0.75 any-hit@3. Third, it is a reproducible signature (split-half self-retrieval approx. 0.97$). Finally, these findings are consistent across seven base models (Qwen2.5 0.5-7B, Llama-3 1-8B), with a suggestive trend of alignment rising with MMLU accuracy. The spectral fingerprint thus provides a probe of how transformers process different topics across depth. Code is available at https://github.com/DeepK/koopman-llm-eacl27.

title: Bridging Blind Spots With Words: Decentralized Multi-View Spatial Reasoning via Language-Constrained Communication
text: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we first formalize the general problem of decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning, where N agents observe distinct viewpoints, exchange budget-constrained natural language messages, and collaborate to enable a listener to answer spatial queries. We then introduce a novel multi-view spatial benchmark to isolate queries that demand non-trivial multi-view integration. Through an extensive empirical study, we discover that the penalty of restricting decentralized spatial reasoning to natural language with limited budget is far smaller than suggested by prior two-agent literature. Nevertheless, we observe that substantial headroom still remains for multi-agent spatial reasoning in this setting, as evidenced by a significant gap between current centralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling. Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.

title: Beyond Evidence Coverage: Encoding-Time Access in Multi-Agent Systems
text: Cache-sharing multi-agent systems can retain every evidence token's representation while preventing cross-worker access during encoding. We test whether this coverage recovers joint-encoding quality using attention masks over two logical workers in frozen Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models. Tokens, positions, and answer-time access remain fixed within comparisons. We evaluate 200 two-hop MuSiQue-Ans questions and 200 selected HotpotQA bridge questions. In data-layout seed 0, averaged across models, blocking access costs 5.6 and 6.8 F1 points relative to full access on MuSiQue and HotpotQA, respectively. Exposing the earlier worker's supporting paragraph improves F1 over blocked access by 7.6 and 6.7 points; equal-token non-support access provides no detectable average gain. With model weights and greedy decoding fixed, we vary distractor layouts using five data-layout seeds per dataset for Qwen3-8B and three for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Supporting-paragraph access has higher mean F1 than blocked and equal-token non-support access in every evaluated data-layout seed. Supporting access can also outperform full access, but its advantage depends on the model, dataset, and layout. Oracle support labels isolate access from selection error; the study does not evaluate a deployable selector. Complete evidence coverage at answer time therefore does not guarantee joint-encoding quality: which supporting facts can interact during encoding matters.

title: Spatial Ensemble Logic for Biomedical Imaging: Geometric Element Ensembles in Euclidean Space
text: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics over metric monoids whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We study its member over the Euclidian space, called Spatial Ensemble Logic (SEL), for biomedical images. Geometric element ensembles (GELs) represent atomic propositions by finite lists of effectively presented semi-algebraic sets, principally closed balls. Translation, dilation and erosion preserve individual balls up to emptiness in any dimension. Translation and dilation act element-wise, but element-wise erosion gives only an inner bound. For $k\geq 2$, finite unions of balls are closed under neither intersection nor erosion. We therefore separate record representation from the evaluation domain. Our main result is a satisfaction-preserving translation over GELs into the first-order theory of real closed fields. It yields computable semi-algebraic satisfaction sets, decidable model checking and finite real algebraic evidence. For a fixed formula and dimension, model checking has polynomial data complexity under stated rationality and bounded-degree assumptions. Combined complexity is PSPACE-hard and in EXPSPACE. On the line, rational interval data admit linear-arithmetic evaluation with rational evidence, under rationality assumptions on the norm, query and evaluation point. For $k\geq 2$, rational balls can force irrational witnesses. Lower and upper annotation bounds propagate through formulas. Synthesis of a ball ensemble is decidable within a prescribed budget of balls and undecidable without one. In a vascular use case, medial ball ensembles decide calibre and stenosis queries at stored centers by comparing stored numbers. We also examine how far evaluation can proceed element-wise when the union forming a support is deferred to the point of evaluation.

title: Beyond Free-Form Generation: Measuring Interface Composition in Competitive NLP Systems
text: Systems with decoder LLMs can combine free generation with scoring, ranking, or selection. We measure these documented interface combinations with five annotation fields linked to source evidence. The corpora comprise 517 solutions from 42 Kaggle competitions involving NLP and 76 participant systems from 26 SemEval, TREC, and WMT task years. Among eligible generation systems with decoder LLMs, 18 of 55 Kaggle systems and 17 of 20 Shared Task systems are hybrid: free generation coexists with a constrained interface. The remaining systems use free generation alone. Giving each competition or task year equal weight yields hybrid shares of 0.327 and 0.876. Within Eedi, 21 eligible systems with decoder LLMs have five exact interface profiles; ten LLM Science Exam systems share one interface class and have four profiles. Across Kaggle, the eligible systems with decoder LLMs span 18 exact interface profiles, revealing variation within broad task and backbone categories. These estimates characterize documented public systems selected using our selection criteria and include interfaces throughout the complete pipeline, including intermediate stages. The data are available at https://github.com/xiaoxinchenn/nlp-interface-composition.

title: DUO Policy: Bridging Human Video Coverage and Robot Precision for Fine-Grained Manipulation
text: Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. Project Webpage: https://mingxi-jia.github.io/duo_policy_site/

title: Neural Costate Guidance for Autonomous Cislunar Low-Thrust Trajectory Generation
text: Future missions will benefit from onboard autonomous low-thrust trajectory generation to correct deviations from the nominal flight path caused by navigation errors and thruster outages. Onboard computing resources rarely allow the solution of a cold-started, long-duration nonconvex optimal control problem, especially in dynamically challenging regions such as the cislunar to translunar corridor of the Earth-Moon system. This paper develops data augmentation and training techniques that enable a neural network to predict accurate initial costates of the indirect method. A recovery trajectory is then built from repeated network queries in a computationally efficient guidance algorithm. Training data are produced by the backward generation of optimal examples method, extending prior approaches to the circular restricted three-body problem. A novel anchor trajectory approach is developed to cover the relevant state space, and costate rescaling and a Hamiltonian loss term are used to improve learning. The method is demonstrated on Earth-Moon transfers from a high Earth orbit to halo orbits about L1 and L2. Under navigation errors and thruster outages, a spacecraft reaches the target orbit more often with the proposed method than with nominal-trajectory tracking or fully numerical reoptimization. Onboard computation is reduced by more than an order of magnitude compared with reoptimization.

title: TesseraFlow: Scalable Video Diffusion for Dynamic Medical Imaging Inverse Problems
text: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.

title: Operational Runbooks as Living Documents: A Longitudinal Study of Document Evolution under Assisted Post-Incident Revision
text: Operational runbooks increasingly function as living documents within operational workflows: they are maintained by people, used in incident support, and continuously revised as organizational knowledge changes. Yet little is known about how such document collections evolve over time in production settings, or which interpretable signals are useful for monitoring document change. We analyze 17 weeks of version-controlled runbook snapshots produced during post-incident revision with machine-assisted review and human oversight. We quantify document evolution using lightweight linguistic and structural signals grounded in prior work on procedural language, technical communication, and document organization. Correlation analysis shows mixed patterns of association, including both positive and negative relationships, with effect sizes ranging from negligible to moderate and varying across corpora. Temporal summaries further distinguish comparatively stable signals from revision-sensitive ones, supporting monitoring of document maintenance workflows rather than one-shot quality judgments. An illustrative analysis on public GitHub product documentation shows that signal behavior differs across corpora, reinforcing the need for context-aware interpretation. These results identify which metric classes provide stable anchors and which provide edit-sensitive indicators for managing operational documentation as an engineered document resource.

title: JEPA-Tuner: From Predictive Fine-Tuning to Asynchronous Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.

title: HME-PFD: Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation
text: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, facilitating efficient serving of machine learning systems. In the context of ads recommendation, privileged features distillation (PFD) extends KD by allowing the teacher model to leverage privileged features, i.e., features available only during training, to enhance distillation performance. However, in real-world scenarios, privileged features often have limited coverage and exhibit heterogeneous distributions, resulting in training examples of varying importance for distillation and model learning. We propose Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation (HME-PFD), a novel approach that incorporates privileged features into the routing module of a Mixture-of-Experts-based student model. Our method introduces both hard-coded and learnable routing modules, enabling the student to dynamically determine expert assignment based on the availability and values of privileged features. This design allows the student model to better handle the heterogeneous data scenario, where privileged features are partially observed, by differentiating between high- and low-signal samples. Extensive experiments on two post-click conversion prediction tasks demonstrate that HME-PFD consistently outperforms baseline methods. Our results show that leveraging privileged features for expert routing in the student model leads to improved model performance, even when privileged features are incomplete or sparse.

title: Seeing the Invisible: How Vision-Language Models Read, Predict and Trace Radio Fields
text: Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.

title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
text: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.

title: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study
text: Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model's prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert's skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill's text. Project repository: https://github.com/LitaoGuo/How-Self-Evolution-Reshapes-Skills.

title: Which Dwarf Is This? Doppeldwarf-306 and Near-Identical Instance Retrieval
text: Most established instance-retrieval benchmarks emphasise landmarks; small sculptures from visually similar series offer a complementary challenge. We introduce Doppeldwarf-306: 1,691 openly licensed photographs of 306 bronze dwarf statues in Wrocław, Poland, many made in themed series that share one style, with the photographer of each image recorded. With no training, nearest-neighbour search over frozen DINOv2 features names the right statue first for 93.1% of leave-one-out queries, and the best of thirteen backbones from seven pretraining paradigms reaches 94.7%. Accuracy falls slowly as candidates are added: for DINOv2, by about 0.8 points each time their number doubles. A natural design for a phone guide compares a photograph only with statues near the user. In simulation this helps, but less than an equal number of randomly chosen statues does, so random subsampling overstates its value; a permutation test ties the penalty to the real layout (p = 0.005). Used as a weight instead of a filter, location raises DINOv2 from 93.4% to 98.7% for a simulated user 25 m from the statue. With the query's photographer withheld, learned local-feature matching raises DINOv2 accuracy from 81.8% to 85.5% and also improves DINOv3. Comparing the two best candidates cuts DINOv2's false acceptance of unknown statues from 38.3% to 19.6% at 90% known acceptance.

title: Autoregressive View Model
text: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.

title: Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds
text: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project

title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
text: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
text: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.

title: Self-WSP: Can Language Models Improve Themselves Through Weight-Space Programming?
text: Frontier language models can now read and edit the weights of a neural network much like code and thereby improve a small model, an approach known as Weight-Space Programming (WSP). We further explore applying WSP to a language model itself, which we call Self-WSP. Specifically, Qwen3.5-0.8B reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and then continues with the edited weights as both problem solver and editor. We find many cases of genuine self-improvement. Self-edits can raise GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%, sometimes by changing only 16 parameters, and in some cases repeated self-editing keeps improving the model. A closer look, however, reveals that these gains lack interpretability. The model shows little understanding of the edits it makes, and WSP driven by random search sometimes performs comparably. Self-WSP thus holds promise as a path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), but realizing this promise requires further exploration.

title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
text: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.

title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
text: An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test⁠(opens in a new window), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements. The Shirudo technical walkthrough⁠(opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host⁠(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here⁠(opens in a new window). Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer. Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. title: Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days
text: Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol to equip its AI support agents with tools and procedures, and GPT‑6 Luna for their conversations. Beyond knowing how to answer a customer’s request, AI support agents need to be able to execute a solution. And for that, they need access to the right tools and instructions. According to Richpanel CEO Amit RG, human support agents can use 20 or 30 tools to serve a customer, and the procedures they follow may never have been written down. Richpanel⁠(opens in a new window) solves that using OpenAI models to both set up the tools and procedures AI support agents need to act and handle customer conversations. “The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it.” Building the tools and procedures for AI support Deploying a support agent often requires a forward-deployed engineer to connect the agent to a customer’s systems and define how it should work. Amit saw that many companies didn’t have engineers to spare and asked himself, “What if that forward-deployed engineer itself was an AI agent?” So Richpanel built it: an AI manager to handle agent setup. Customers began calling it Boss AI. It writes procedures and defines how Richpanel’s frontline support agent, copilot, and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need. Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow. It uses GPT‑6 Luna and other OpenAI models for that work. Amit says Richpanel takes the same approach to its copilot and quality-assurance agents. “What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence,” Amit says. Richpanel’s customers may already use low-cost outsourced support. Automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point. Amit credits OpenAI with making models available that can handle long context and longer tasks while remaining cost efficient. Richpanel can use deeper reasoning to prepare its support agents and more economical models to run the conversations that follow. Increasing contact center automation and customer satisfaction At the time of the October 2026 interview, Amit said Richpanel had completed approximately 300 AI customer-support deployments over the previous six months. The company guarantees customers a 50% automation rate within the first 30 days or their money back. title: Developing-Gamer/agent-sim: iOS simulators for AI agents, on Linux
text: iOS simulators for AI agents, on Linux. agent-sim iOS simulators for AI agents, on ordinary Linux machines. No Mac, no GPU. Safari on Apple's iOS runtime, on a Linux VM, recorded at 60 fps (the GIF is 15). Full clip · An agent driving Settings and Safari agent-sim runs Apple's iOS simulator runtime on an x86-64 Linux VM and gives agents what they need to test iOS apps: install an .ipa, read the screen as text, tap, type, scroll, and watch it live in a browser. One command line for scripts and CI, and an MCP server for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and other agents. Status: early. It works end to end; expect rough edges, and see what does not work yet. Quick start On an x86-64 Linux machine with Ubuntu 24.04 (8+ CPUs, 16 GB of memory, 60 GB of free disk): From a checkout instead: cargo build --release, then scripts/setup-vm.sh and target/release/agent-sim. agent-sim setup --fidelity high --device hifi adds a phone that looks exactly like Apple's simulator (3x, every blur and animation) for screenshots; the default draws at 2x with reduced effects and scrolls twice as fast. Use it from an agent As an MCP server: An agent on another machine (your laptop) runs the same server over SSH; MCP's stdio passes through unchanged: The tools are snapshot, tap, type, scroll, swipe, press, launch, terminate, install, uninstall, apps, openurl, waitfor, screenshot and boot. Actions answer with the screen that follows, so an agent sees the result of each step without asking again. For agents that work in a shell, skills/agent-sim/SKILL.md teaches the command line. The command line snapshot reads the accessibility tree of the app in front, the web pages it shows, and SpringBoard, so system alerts, the home screen and the status bar are in it too. Every command takes --device NAME; agent-sim --help lists them all. The simulator controls Apple's simctl has are here too: appearance dark, status-bar --time 9:41, clipboard, record -o video.mp4, erase, logs, plus x86Sim's location, push, privacy and addmedia. docs/PARITY.md compares every feature with Apple's Simulator on a Mac. Device builds run when they are not encrypted. App Store downloads are (FairPlay), so use an Ad Hoc, Development or Enterprise export, or build for the simulator. Watch it in a browser It prints a URL with an access token. The page streams the screen as H.264 over a WebSocket (decoded with WebCodecs, so a recent Chrome, Edge or Safari) and sends touches, keys, scrolling and the Home and Lock buttons back. Touches that start at a screen edge are system gestures: a swipe up from the bottom goes home. Keep the token private. Many phones Phones share memory through the kernel's KSM: three take 6.8 GB together instead of 8.7 GB. On a cloud provider with VM memory snapshots, a booted phone can be saved and brought back running in about 20 seconds (docs/BENCHMARKS.md). How it works x86Sim runs Apple's arm64 simulator runtime on x86-64 Linux: Darling provides the macOS kernel interfaces, dynarmic translates the ARM code, and Mesa's CPU Vulkan driver draws Metal through metal2vulkan. agent-sim builds the agent-facing product on top of it: A phone set up for speed: a pre-translated runtime, the services apps need and none they do not, the screen drawn at 2x, and reduced transparency and motion. Scrolling runs at about 55 fps on a Zen 5 VM, and a touch reaches the screen in about 14 ms (docs/BENCHMARKS.md). Fixes in x86Sim (patches/x86sim): web workers in Safari, and apps with crash reporters no longer crawl. Hooks in the phone (hooks): an accessibility reader for snapshot, and stale permission prompts dismissed as on a device. The agent interface: the CLI, the MCP server, .ipa conversion, the phone pool and the browser stream. Documentation docs/PARITY.md: feature by feature against Apple's Simulator on a Mac docs/BENCHMARKS.md: speed, memory, several phones, snapshots docs/KNOWNISSUES.md: what does not work yet and why docs/ROADMAP.md: what comes next CONTRIBUTING.md and SECURITY.md Credits agent-sim builds on x86Sim, which runs Apple's simulator runtimes on Linux through Darling, dynarmic and metal2vulkan. Fixes agent-sim needs in x86Sim itself live in patches/x86sim until they are upstream. Apple's runtimes are downloaded from Apple onto your own machine and are never part of this repository.
